idiom_name: this-modifier extension methods / C# 14 extension blocks
implementation_notes: The C# servant is a non-nested, non-generic static class holding extension members: a static method whose first parameter carries the this modifier (C# 3) or an extension block (C# 14) that can also declare properties, operators and static members. LINQ's Enumerable is the framework's own servant: every IEnumerable<T> gains query operations without any class implementing them. Extension members are bound statically, cannot see private state, and lose to an instance member with the same signature, so the classic static servant class is still the right form when the serviced type must be substituted in tests or the servant carries state.
pitfalls: Extension members are resolved at compile time with lower priority than real members: a later instance method with the same signature silently takes over, so behaviour can change without any change at the call site.

They cannot touch private state, and calling one on a null receiver is legal: the null reference is passed straight into the servant, so the NullReferenceException - if any - is raised inside it and the stack trace points at the servant rather than at the caller.
sources: Microsoft Learn, Extension members (C# programming guide) - this-modifier syntax, C# 14 extension blocks, binding rules and LINQ as the canonical use; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/extension-methods

Microsoft Learn, extension keyword (C# language reference) - extension block syntax, receiver semantics and binary compatibility with the classic form; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/extension

variants.name: Static servant class (classic form)
variants.idiom_name: static class of static methods taking the serviced object as an argument
variants.implementation_notes: The classic structure translated literally: a static class whose methods take the serviced object as their first argument, called as Servant.Operation(serviced, ...). It cannot be shadowed by an instance member, needs no using-directive to become available, can be internal to the assembly, and keeps the behaviour off the serviced type's IntelliSense surface - which is why framework internals and validation-style services are still written this way. Prefer it when the servant must be visible to callers without adding members to a type you do not own, or when an extension member would be misleading because the operation reads better when it names the servant explicitly.
pitfalls: Static methods cannot be substituted, so any test that exercises a caller must go through the real behaviour; inject an interface-backed servant instead once the behaviour talks to I/O or configuration.
Because nothing scopes it, the static class is where unrelated helpers accumulate; keep one static servant per cohesive service rather than an assembly-wide Utilities class.
sources: Microsoft Learn, How to implement and call a custom extension method - states that adding the functionality to the type itself or deriving is preferable, which is the boundary between the static servant and the extension member; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/how-to-implement-and-call-a-custom-extension-method
